parts.note: holiness is traditionally said to give off a sweet smell, the 'odour' of the saints, so the whole clue describes saintliness

explanation.surface: A woman called Grace wears perfume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grace' looks like a woman's name; it is the quality of holiness, and the scent is the proverbial odour of saints.
explanation.definitionFit: Holiness or saintliness, a state of divine grace, is what the word names.

explanation.surface: Someone obtained something and strengthened it.
explanation.definitionFit: Obtaining something is getting hold of it, and making a fort safe against attack is protecting it.

parts.note: plays on the old saying 'as right as' a small old coin, meaning perfectly well, read as a sum of money

explanation.surface: A remark that the accounts are in order.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom 'right as ninepence' means in perfect order; the coin was a pre-decimal amount of money.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sum of nine pennies features in the idiom for being perfectly all right.

clue.text: Heroic bull-fighter in the lower right corner of America

parts.note: on a map the lower right corner is the south-east, SE
US is the United States of America

explanation.surface: A matador hero is found in the far south-east of the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The bull is the Minotaur, killed by the Greek hero in the Cretan labyrinth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian hero of Greek myth slew the half-bull Minotaur in the labyrinth.

definitions.meaning: a totter is British slang for a rag-and-bone man, a scrap collector, so the word is read as resembling one

explanation.surface: A scrap collector who wobbles on his feet.
explanation.walkthrough: A rag-and-bone man is a British street collector of old junk, also called a totter.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaky and wobbling on one's feet, likely to stagger, is how the word is normally used.

indicators.note: the fish goes around the bird, enclosing it

parts.note: the cod is a fish
pie is an old name for the magpie

explanation.surface: A fish swims round and a bird comes after it.
explanation.walkthrough: PIE, the magpie, is a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow someone's example is to imitate them, the same idea as reproducing their work.

clue.text: Sort of airman in a conveyance .

indicators.note: the airman sits inside the conveyance

parts.note: a charter is a deed conveying rights
AC is an aircraftman, a junior airman

explanation.surface: Some kind of pilot sits in a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: AC (aircraftman) is the lowest RAF rank; 'conveyance' looks like a vehicle but is a document granting rights.
explanation.definitionFit: Character means a kind or type of person, as in 'a shady sort'.

clue.text: … more corpulent one in a railway engine

indicators.note: one is placed inside the engine

parts.note: a puffer is a child's word for a steam engine
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A fatter man rides in a steam locomotive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puffer' is nursery talk for a steam train.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffy means swollen or plump, so the comparative means fatter.

clue.text: As girl slept, he moved out

indicators.note: the letters are moved out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A man left while a young woman was asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moved out' looks like leaving the house; it rearranges SLEPT HE.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish form of Elizabeth used as a woman's first name.

parts.note: acting in concert is acting in union, so union means concert
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people find togetherness in a tight hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squeeze' looks like a verb or a hug; it is the squeezebox, a small hand-held instrument with bellows.
explanation.definitionFit: The squeezebox is a familiar name for this small bellows instrument played between the hands.

clue.text: Safety device in a train that sets off

definitions.meaning: an electrical cut-out that melts when the current is too high
a line of powder or cord that carries the flame to an explosive charge

explanation.surface: A railway carriage carries safety equipment for departure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' suggests a railway; here it is a line of combustible material leading to a charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the household cut-out and the burning cord that ignites a bomb share this word.

definitions.meaning: standing as a symbol or typical example of something
an old word for an agent who acts on another's behalf

explanation.surface: A question about whether something is a symbolic element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'factor' looks mathematical; it is an agent, as in a Scottish estate factor.
explanation.definitionFit: Something typical or symbolic is this, and so is an agent or delegate acting for others.

clue.text: Ruling line to differentiate any non-university study

indicators.note: differentiating changes things, so the letters are worked into a new order
the letter for university is to be removed from the word that follows

parts.note: taken as written before its letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A family dynasty seeks to set apart any study done outside a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-university' drops U (university) from STUDY to leave STDY; 'to differentiate' then rearranges ANY with STDY.
explanation.definitionFit: A succession of rulers from one family forms a hereditary line of monarchs.

definitions.meaning: awkward with the hands, as if all thumbs
able to use both hands equally

explanation.surface: Someone is awkward despite using both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The word once meant both clumsy and able to fight with either hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Having two fists suggests both awkward hands and the use of both hands alike.

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
archy is the free-verse-typing cockroach in Don Marquis's archy and mehitabel

explanation.surface: Someone stiffly proper deals with a cockroach.
explanation.walkthrough: archy is the cockroach hero of Don Marquis's comic poems, who typed without capitals.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff and formal behaviour is called starchy, like a starched collar, so it fits conventional.

parts.note: a seat made of the rod once used for beating pupils, read as the place where a caning lands

explanation.surface: Where a punished pupil sits.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'seat' is both a chair and the backside, where a school beating landed.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattan chair, woven from the same stems as a punishment rod.

clue.text: Sort of square to argue it's a crime

parts.note: a T-square is a kind of drawing square
to reason is to argue a case

explanation.surface: Someone claims that being old-fashioned is criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square' suggests a fuddy-duddy; it is the T-square used in technical drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: Betraying one's country is the gravest offence against the state.

clue.text: Rest, in lifting about outstanding art work

indicators.note: the rest goes inside the turned word
in a down clue lifting reads the word upwards, so backwards

parts.note: over means about, as in a dispute over pay
to lie is to rest

explanation.surface: A break in heavy lifting is spent around a prominent sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifting' reverses OVER to REVO in this down clue; LIE goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised sculpture that stands out from its background is relief work.

clue.text: Do better, in a way, in opposition

indicators.note: the improvement goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
to gain is to improve or do better

explanation.surface: Improve somewhat, as a rival.
explanation.definitionFit: Being opposed to something is being set against it.

clue.text: The Gunners dined in mess and drank up

indicators.note: being in a mess means jumbled up, so the gunners and dined are mixed together

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners

explanation.surface: Artillerymen ate in their mess hall and finished their drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in mess' looks like the soldiers' dining room; it signals an anagram of RA (Royal Artillery) with DINED.
explanation.definitionFit: To drain a glass is to empty it completely, finishing every drop.

clue.text: Bother about false gen — it's a trap

indicators.note: the exclamation goes around the jumbled letters

parts.note: drat and bother are both mild exclamations of annoyance

indicators.note: false information is distorted, so the letters of gen are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fake intelligence is a nuisance and a snare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gen' is British slang for information; 'false' rearranges it to GNE, and 'about' puts DRAT around that.
explanation.definitionFit: A net dragged through water or a systematic police search catches everything in its path.

clue.text: A professional performer one treats differently

indicators.note: arranged differently, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A stage pro handles people in an unusual way.
explanation.definitionFit: A paid entertainer, singer or dancer is described with this French-derived word.

parts.note: due means expected, as in the train is due

indicators.note: in a down clue rising reads the word upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded valley

explanation.surface: A battle had been anticipated as the valley rose.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people fighting a formal combat with swords or pistols took part in a duel.

definitions.meaning: the word a is the indefinite article and comes first, so it is an article that leads
a newspaper editorial giving the paper's view

explanation.surface: Perhaps a newspaper's top item is an opinion piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' looks like a throwaway word; it is the example, a grammatical article coming first.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is the newspaper's main opinion piece, and a or the is a grammatical article placed before nouns.

explanation.surface: A sharp-cornered curve.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaunt, bony person is thin, and to tilt or incline the body is to bend.

clue.text: It is thrown into service in new-style ballet perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests a possible version, so the letters are arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written
NS is the abbreviation for New Style, the Gregorian calendar dating

explanation.surface: A dancer is drafted into a modern ballet production.
explanation.walkthrough: N.S. (New Style) marks dates in the reformed calendar; it sits between IN and BALLET, and 'perhaps' shuffles all three.
explanation.definitionFit: A server tosses this up and strikes it to start each point on court.

parts.note: to boot something is to kick it
Ed is a boy's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A lad who was kicked out has been given his notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sacked and sent away with final wages is being dismissed, kicked out of the job.

parts.note: Ethel is a girl's name
an embarrassed person goes red

explanation.surface: A blushing young woman is shamed by an elderly monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Ethelred the Unready was an Anglo-Saxon English monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Two Anglo-Saxon English monarchs bore this name, the best known being the Unready.
